summary: A Common Sense Media study tracked smartphone use among 203 kids aged 11 to 17 and found phones are a "constant companion," with 97% using them during school hours and nearly 60% overnight on school nights. Social media, especially TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram, dominated screen time, and many under-13s accessed age-inappropriate apps. Experts Jennifer Kelman and Shelley Delayne warn about social, developmental and safety risks and advise delaying phone access and monitoring content.
one_line: A Common Sense Media study of 203 kids aged 11-17 finds 97% use phones during school, prompting expert advice to delay and monitor phone access.
key_facts: Common Sense Media, a nonprofit group in San Francisco, California, studied phone usage among 203 kids aged 11 to 17.
Kids spent a median of 4.5 hours per day on their phones, with a maximum of 16 hours.
Teens checked their phones from two to 498 times per day; adolescents were more likely to check over 100 times a day.
97% of kids used their phones during school hours, and nearly 60% used them overnight between midnight and 5 a.m. on school nights.
Social media such as Instagram and Snapchat took up 32% of screen time during the school day, followed by YouTube and gaming.
More than 50% of kids get 237 notifications per day, some as many as 4,500; about 23% occur during school hours.
TikTok was used by half of participants for nearly two hours per day on average, with some scrolling up to seven hours; the longest time on Snapchat and Instagram was about three hours daily.
Of 85 participants under age 13, 68% used social media and had at least one app rated "teen" or higher.
Nearly half (45%) of participants used apps with mature or adult-only ratings, such as porn sites, fantasy sports and betting apps.
More than two-thirds of participants said managing tech use is sometimes or often difficult or that they use it to escape negative feelings, and they reported missing sleep.
Licensed clinical social worker Jennifer Kelman warned phones trigger the same dopamine release as drugs and advised delaying phone access as long as possible.
Kelman suggested a kid-safe starter phone like Pinwheel, which has no internet and only parent-approved apps.
Shelley Delayne of Pinwheel recommended delaying adult online spaces and social media to age 16 or older.
The study used software to collect data from Android phone users only, because Apple device tracking does not share names of specific non-Apple apps.
